# Olde Weirde?s Incunabulum

*Pages PDF 4-7*

## Olde Weirde’s Incunabulum
I had been spending the morning ensuring that my upcoming series of lectures on the carnivorous flora of Lustria coincided with Professor Pfaff’s lessons on the supremacy of Sigmar when I was informed that my efforts had been wasted, as dear old Pfaff had taken a bad dose of the Yellow Ague. 

The pious fool is too small-minded to seek the healing hands of Shallya’s priests, claiming that the disease had been sent to test his mettle and, I quote his exact words here, ‘just as the rebarbative Ironjaw was vanquished in the first battle of Blackfire Pass, when the multifarious goblin coalitions recklessly ranked in league vendetta against our heroic holy founder, so shall I beat this contumacious xanthic ailment’. With that attitude he is sure to be confined to his bed for the whole of the upcoming semester, and no doubt have plenty of time to improve his repertoire of pretentious adjectives. 

Now, privately I was heartened to realise Pfaff’s illness would spare the scholars of the University fifteen weeks of the same sanctimonious charlatanry any resident of Altdorf can receive for free by attending Festag musters at the Grand Cathedral. However, I did reflect on the loss to the world that might result from the illness or death of a more profound thinker. 

It strikes me that Pfaff’s attitude towards dealing with the disease — the notion that to suffer it is to embrace a tempering process from which he shall emerge stronger and more resilient — is less typical of the attitudes of true Sigmarites, but has more in common with one of the greatest heresies a person can commit. It has all the appearance of the core beliefs of the Plague God, who delights in the gift of disease and whose followers wholeheartedly believe that which does not kill you somehow also fails to debase, debilitate, and damage you. 

Which, of course, is all disease does. And the Cult of Sigmar is wise enough to recognise this and earnestly encourages its congregants to seek solace at the temple of Shallya should they suffer from so much as a runny nose. 

The followers of the Plague God are corrupt and their motives insane. Who would condemn themselves to such a loathsome existence? Any creature that has entered his service inevitably becomes host to cankers, agues, parasites, infections, and other afflictions. The corruption of their bodies is plain to see. Thrice-damned adherents of this mad cult are instantly recognised by their scabrous skin, constellations of boils and pox marks, their doomed flesh rent through with weeping lesions and sores. 

WARBAND OF BAYL OF MANY EYES 

Yet those who venerate the Plague God do not mind these disfigurements and even bear them with pride. I’ve read numerous sources claiming they do not exhibit any sign of suffering from ailments, indeed, they are said to be cheerful and energetic despite evident grotesque corporeal corruption. 

Much of my research into the practices and beliefs of these forsaken wretches is taken from _Liber Malefic, the Book of Chaos Foreseen_ , collected by Marius Hollseher and published in 1778 IC. This collection of material drawn from interrogations of captured cultists and marauders, as well as testimony from those who have ventured into the Chaos Wastes and survived with their sanity somewhat intact. 

The work is not yet proscribed, though to dedicate too much time to reading it no doubt arouses suspicion. Professor Pfaff, of course, claims that to study the work is a certain way to end up being dragged, screaming, into the charnel houses of the Chaos Hells, there to writhe in endless debate with the flames and the daemons of torment. Whilst I fear to say so in public, I suspect his is an old-fashioned view and most scholars respect the need to understand a modicum of the practises of the followers of the Ruinous Powers to oppose them. 

Hollseher himself is known to have journeyed to the edges of the wastes on more than one occasion. An expert in the translation of the runes of the Dark Tongue spoken by Beastmen and other followers of Chaos, he has translated many monoliths and inscriptions, providing invaluable, if disturbing, insights. 

One of the most informative monuments lies on the north coast of the Sea of Chaos. It is a slab of flinty stone crudely etched with carved runes, dedicated to Goresqualor, considered a Champion among those who venerate the ruinous powers. According to Hollseher they explain the origin of Goresqualor, his achievements, the gifts of Chaos that he received during his life, and the facts of his death. Regarding his early life the monolith has this to say: 

A youngster alone in the woods would need reserves of endurance only Nurgle could give them. Later the monolith states: 

_I was home to Nurgle’s mites My little friends went with me everywhere I slew many and bestowed the rot on many more_ 

The monolith describes many gifts granted by Nurgle to Goresqualor. This stanza describes what I presume to be an infestation of tiny imps common to the followers of Nurgle. 

Whilst all the dreadful gods of Chaos are associated with different forms of Daemon, both great and small, Nurgle is known for the myriad diminutive daemons  who serve him and bear the palanquins awarded to his favoured Champions. 

Goresqualor seems to have become a haven for such creatures, and rather than finding such an infestation repellent he seems happy with the arrangement, calling them his ‘friends’. 

He boasts, as do most Champions of Chaos, of the many foes he slew during his life. However, when it comes to the spreading of disease he uses the language of gift-giving, claiming that he ‘bestowed the rot’. 

This is where I feel Pfaff’s own attitude to disease resembles too closely that of the followers of Nurgle, for they seem to welcome affliction as a test to be overcome, rather than a source of needless waste and misery. His apparent pride in undergoing the ravages of disease therefore mirrors theirs! 

Travelling north from the monolith of Goresqualor one can find the monolith of Lothar Bubonicus the Exalted. This Champion of Nurgle may have pleased the Maggot Lord to an even greater degree than Goresqualor, for if his saga is to be believed he did not perish upon the field of battle but was raised to Nurgle’s daemonic court. The vile inscription begins thusly: 

_They abandoned me in the forest I was a child marked by Nurgle. A beast they said, and a beast I was, My own kind found me and protected me I learned the ways of Nurgle_ 

Apparently Goresqualor was born to human parents and visibly mutated. The mother and father were unwilling to hand this snot-nosed starveling over to the witch hunters and left him in the woods. Perhaps even at this young age the child really was marked by the Plague God, but it is just as likely that the reason Goresqualor came to praise him above the other Ruinous Powers is hinted at with the word ‘protection’. Many of Nurgle’s followers honour him for the resilience he grants them. 

_When the Green Death raged I swore an oath to Father Nurgle. I bade him spare me that I might live in his service And Father Nurgle chose me as his own. Though all the village perished I alone survived._ 

So, it seems that Lothar was grown enough to be capable of making decisions of his own when he began his life as a Champion of Nurgle. 

I note that in beseeching the Plague God to save him from the Green Death Lothar admits that disease can kill and debilitate in a way that Goresqualor does not. I wonder if the god takes affront at those in his service who conceed the disastrous effects of disease, or whether he shows preference for those who call upon him to deliver them from sickness, or whether he does not care. If the tales have it true, Lothar is far from alone in seeking succour from disease by appealing to Nurgle, yet the attitude that disease is a gift to be bestowed is widespread among his worshippers. 

In other respects, Lothar’s words and attitude mirror those of Goresqualor, such as when he too is made a host to imps. 

_For me, mites of Nurgle, my little friends. To lick my sores._ 

The saga of Lothar is particularly fascinating, as it gives us an insight into cultural practices followed by the worshippers of Nurgle, as the following stanza implies a form of prophetic practice involving observing the movements of vermin. 

_Profane ones violated our sacred woods With foul relics in their train Nurgle told us in the dance of flies_ 

And later: 

_I saw a vision of Nurgle’s realm. A green wood stretching as far as the eye could see Seething with life and the drone of fat flies. When I awoke, I saw the rune of Nurgle in snail-trails. We followed, seeking for the runes Until we crossed the edge of fate._ 

According to the saga Lothar obediently followed these signs for ‘twice twenty years’ before he found the green wood. There he fought his last battle and, according to his saga, won the right to sit at the right-hand side of his loathsome deity. Interestingly the saga once again speaks of disease as something to be transcended, even escaped, through the worship of Nurgle. 

_Nurgle rewarded us For only the worthy may enter his realm. The road was long. Suffering I endured in Nurgle’s name. He did not desert me._ 

_Beside this stone I shed the rags of plague An exalted one of Nurgle, rewarded with immortal flesh._ 

Perhaps it is folly to look for consistency amongst those insane enough to worship the dark gods, but the testimony of the saga of Lothar seems to suggest that he felt no need to regard disease as a pleasant thing to endure. 

However, another stanza within the saga hints at employing disease as a tool of vengeance and using secret agents to do it. 

_Into the city we came at night. Through the sewers we were led by Nurgle’s scouts. Vermin of valour who did their work well. Now the high lords scratch and wither. The justice of Nurgle is delivered._ 

I have no certainty as to what event this portion of the saga refers to, or what is meant by ‘Nurgle’s scouts - vermin of valour’. The stanza would seem to refer to a disease which broke out in a town, and which targeted the wealthy rather than the poor. 

However, I beg to speculate a little here. Lothar’s monolith was discovered under a mound of moss-covered skeletons during Hollseher’s 1760 IC expedition. The town of Uberaverglau in Ostland became a noted site of insurrection and plague in 1702 IC. The noble lords of the town were besieged by their own populace and, confined to their cramped mansions, succumbed to a particularly dangerous strain of the itching pox. This event does align with the symptoms of scratching and withering, and the timing of the event is plausible, giving Lothar forty years to wander the wilderness, and further time for those sacrificed at the unveiling of his monolith to become moss-covered skeletons. 

Ostland is not so far, speaking relatively, from the Troll Country, and, as I have discussed in my edition of the Incunabulum that deals with this wasteland, rat-headed Beastmen are reported to be spotted in that area. In recent years sightings of such creatures have been made in Nuln, and, again, their presence seems to correspond with outbreaks of disease. 

Perhaps these creatures are the ‘scouts of Nurgle - vermin of valour’ mentioned in the saga? Every burgher knows to fear the rat as a spreader of disease and corruption — could such creatures really be spies and agents of the forces of Chaos? 

I began this rumination wondering about the attitude the followers of the plague god had to disease itself. I now find myself increasingly unsettled at the thought that Nurgle’s champions may be able to receive prophetic visions and make alliances with forces we have little understanding of. 

Moreover, what I find most galling is the fact that, were I to publish these thoughts under my own name, and openly seek the opinion of other experts on these matters, I would no doubt come under the scrutiny of the likes of Professor Pfaff and must worry about suspicious members of the Order of the Silver Hammer deeming me some flavour of heretic. I must pry a little into Pfaff’s thinking on the matter, but before I see him again, I will place a fresh order for Professor Schneider’s new unguent. 

WARBAND OF BAYL OF MANY EYES
